extracted.intended_audience: machine-learning researchers and practitioners designing or evaluating federated/decentralized learning systems
extracted.subtask_description: Survey and design guidance for federated, fully-decentralized, cross-silo, and split learning systems, with emphasis on algorithmic, privacy, communication, and practical-deployment considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Robustness to limited client availability and unreliable networks
rubrics_metrics.description: Fully decentralized algorithms should be robust to the limited availability of the clients (with clients temporarily unavailable, dropping out or joining during the execution) and limited reliability of the network (with possible message drops).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Schemes need to handle clients being offline or dropping messages; for some special cases (generalized linear models) duality-structured schemes can help, but for deep learning and SGD robustness remains an open question. Design and analysis should consider client churn and message loss.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convergence under non-IID data distributions
rubrics_metrics.description: Understanding the convergence of decentralized/federated SGD in the presence of non-IID local datasets and designing averaging/communication policies that achieve fast convergence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many results exist for single local-update schemes; multiple local-update steps make theoretical analysis more challenging. Existing works (e.g., [467, 280, 469]) provide partial results, but general understanding and design principles remain open problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of network topology and spectral gap on consensus and convergence
rubrics_metrics.description: Well-connected or denser networks encourage faster consensus and yield better theoretical convergence rates that depend on the spectral gap of the network graph.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Denser networks often increase communication delays with node degree. Practical design must balance spectral properties (for faster error convergence) and per-iteration communication delay; methods like MATCHA decompose graphs into matchings to reduce delay while preserving convergence speed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling message drops and asynchrony
rubrics_metrics.description: Decentralized SGD should tolerate message drops and optionally support asynchronous operation where clients become active independently at random times.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Asynchronous algorithms remove need for global synchronization and can improve scalability. Some works show convergence comparable to reliable networks under message drops for complete graphs with fixed drop probabilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local-update steps vs communication frequency trade-off
rubrics_metrics.description: Trade-offs between performing several local update steps before each communication round versus single-update schemes, and the resulting impact on convergence and analysis complexity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Local multiple-step schemes (as in Federated Averaging) reduce communication but complicate theoretical guarantees, especially under non-IID data. Design must consider how many local steps K to take and its effect on convergence and practical runtime.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personalization and trust mechanisms
rubrics_metrics.description: Designing algorithms to learn personalized models for each client (e.g., smoothing parameters across clients with similar tasks) and mechanisms to build trust/handle malicious or unreliable participants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Personalization can be achieved by smoothing model parameters among similar clients or learning the similarity graph jointly. Challenges include robustness to adversaries and designing incentives or mechanism-design approaches without a trusted central server.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gradient compression and quantization for bandwidth-limited clients
rubrics_metrics.description: Applying compressed communication schemes (quantization, sparsification) in decentralized/fully-decentralized settings so as not to harm convergence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Translating centralized compression schemes to decentralized algorithms without degrading convergence is an active area. Alternatively, design optimization algorithms that naturally produce sparse updates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Privacy: preventing reconstruction from shared updates (differential privacy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Preventing any client from reconstructing another client's private data from shared updates while maintaining model utility, typically via differential privacy (DP) or secure aggregation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Local DP (adding noise at client) is standard but often costly in utility. Secure aggregation and shuffling approaches that improve privacy-utility trade-offs in central FL do not easily integrate with fully decentralized algorithms; decentralization itself might amplify DP guarantees under appropriate relaxations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical decentralization via blockchain and smart contracts
rubrics_metrics.description: Using distributed ledgers and smart contracts to decentralize orchestration (e.g., using smart contracts to aggregate models) and to coordinate participants without a central authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Blockchains publicly expose data by default, which can deter participation; mitigations include secure aggregation protocols, staking/penalty mechanisms to discourage dropouts, confidential smart contracts running in secure enclaves, and encrypting aggregated models with participant-held keys.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secure aggregation protocols that handle participant dropouts
rubrics_metrics.description: Secure aggregation that tolerates participant dropout while preserving privacy of individual updates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Protocols like Bonawitz et al. effectively handle dropouts but at increased complexity. Simpler protocols may be possible if dropouts are prevented (e.g., via staking) or if confidential smart contracts/secure enclaves are available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Client-level differential privacy for blockchain-based FL
rubrics_metrics.description: Achieving client-level DP when clients add noise locally before submitting updates to a public blockchain and ensuring the aggregated noise yields the targeted DP guarantee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each client can add Gaussian noise after local updates; the local noise scale should be chosen so aggregated noise achieves the desired client-level DP. Additional protection can be obtained by encrypting the aggregated model and restricting decryption to participants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data partitioning: feature (vertical) vs example (horizontal) partitioning
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognizing whether data across parties is partitioned by features (vertical) or by examples (horizontal) influences architecture and algorithms used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Feature-partitioned settings often require exchanging intermediate results (not model parameters) and use secure multi-party computation or homomorphic encryption. Algorithms are typically dependent on the ML objective (trees, linear/logistic regression, neural nets).

rubrics_metrics.name: Federated transfer learning for partial overlap
rubrics_metrics.description: Approaches for settings where parties share only partial overlap in users or features and leverage transfer learning to collaborate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Existing formulations are limited (e.g., to two clients). These scenarios require specialized algorithms to exploit partial overlaps while preserving privacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incentive mechanisms for honest participation and free-rider mitigation
rubrics_metrics.description: Mechanisms to encourage truthful/honest participation in FL and to prevent free-riding by participants who contribute little but benefit from the final model.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incentives may be monetary or via differential model performance. Designers must consider how to divide earnings/rewards among contributors, link incentives to defenses against adversarial owners, and ensure sustained participation while avoiding free-rider problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differential privacy priorities and threat models in cross-silo FL
rubrics_metrics.description: In cross-silo settings, who is considered an adversary and what privacy guarantees are needed may differ (e.g., final model may only be released to participants).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Threat models should be explicitly considered; local DP may be necessary if clients are the main threat; in other scenarios, user-level or group-level guarantees might be more appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Privacy-preserving cross-silo tensor factorization
rubrics_metrics.description: Performing tensor factorization across sites holding horizontally-partitioned data while keeping data private and sharing only intermediate factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Approaches include ADMM-based methods and elastic averaging SGD (EASGD), with extensions to ensure differential privacy for intermediate factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Split learning via model-layer partitioning and smashed data
rubrics_metrics.description: Split learning splits model execution by layers between clients and server: clients compute forward pass up to a cut layer, send smashed data to the other party, which completes computation; gradients at the cut layer are sent back.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Variants include vanilla and U-shaped split learning (where labels are not shared). This reduces raw-data transfer but transmits activations/gradients whose privacy leakage must be assessed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk of information leakage from communicated activations in split learning
rubrics_metrics.description: Values communicated in split learning (smashed data / activations) can reveal information about underlying raw data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mitigations include NoPeek SplitNN (reducing distance correlation between smashed data and raw inputs), pruning channels in client-side activations, and the need for formal privacy analyses for split learning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taxonomy: feature distribution skew (covariate shift)
rubrics_metrics.description: One non-IID regime where marginal distributions Pi(x) vary across clients, even if conditional P(y|x) is shared (covariate shift).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: handwriting stroke width/slant varies by user. If P(y|x) is common, a single global model learning P(y|x) may still be appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taxonomy: label distribution skew (prior probability shift)
rubrics_metrics.description: A non-IID regime where marginal label distributions Pi(y) differ across clients even if P(x|y) is the same.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: geographic differences lead to different label prevalences. Empirical synthetic non-IID datasets often simulate this via label partitioning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taxonomy: same label, different features (concept drift)
rubrics_metrics.description: A non-IID regime where Pi(x|y) varies across clients though P(y) may be shared — the same label maps to different features for different clients.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include cultural, seasonal, or temporal variations. This may necessitate model designs that accommodate such conditional differences (e.g., personalization).

rubrics_metrics.name: Taxonomy: same features, different label (concept shift)
rubrics_metrics.description: A non-IID regime where Pi(y|x) varies across clients even if P(x) is the same.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Personal preferences or regional differences can cause identical features to have different labels; personalization may be essential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taxonomy: quantity skew / unbalancedness
rubrics_metrics.description: Clients holding vastly different amounts of data, impacting optimization and fairness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Algorithm and objective choices may need to account for per-client dataset sizes, e.g., weighting updates or limiting contributions from large clients.

rubrics_metrics.name: Violations of independence due to changing client distribution Q
rubrics_metrics.description: The distribution over available clients Q may change over training (e.g., diurnal device availability correlated with longitude), violating independence assumptions used in analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These temporal/geographic biases need mitigation (e.g., local shuffling, time-aware model selection); Eichner et al. discuss mitigation strategies, but many open questions remain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dataset shift between training and deployment clients
rubrics_metrics.description: Differences between the clients eligible to participate in training and those where the model will be deployed can cause dataset shift.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: training may require devices with more memory than inference; adapting classical dataset-shift techniques to FL is an open problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategy: augment or share a small global dataset to reduce heterogeneity
rubrics_metrics.description: Creating a small shared dataset (proxy, public dataset, or distilled data) to make client data more similar and aid training of a global model.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shared datasets can be useful where privacy allows; distillation techniques or public proxies can help evaluate and mitigate non-IID effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategy: crafting objective functions to limit per-client dominance and improve fairness
rubrics_metrics.description: Modify the global objective to limit the contributions of any single user and introduce fairness notions across clients.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limiting per-client influence also supports privacy goals; objective design should reflect application-specific fairness and utility trade-offs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategy: personalization / multi-model approaches
rubrics_metrics.description: Instead of forcing a single global model, provide customized models per client (personalization) to address non-IIDness and availability-induced heterogeneity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Personalization can convert non-IID data from a bug to a feature; multi-model approaches or averaging different iterates (e.g., by timezone) can provide models tuned to client subpopulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Optimization requirement: stateless algorithms and client sampling
rubrics_metrics.description: FL algorithms must often be stateless (clients participate rarely) and work with only a handful of sampled clients per round.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This rules out many stateful datacenter algorithms (e.g., ADMM) and compression strategies that rely on maintaining residuals across rounds. Design should assume clients may participate at most once per model training run.

rubrics_metrics.name: Optimization desideratum: composability with secure aggregation, DP, and compression
rubrics_metrics.description: Optimization algorithms should be composable with cryptographic secure aggregation, differential privacy, and compression primitives used in practical deployments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expressing algorithms in terms of primitives like 'sum over selected clients' and 'broadcast to selected clients' aids composability, but may exclude techniques (e.g., certain asynchronous or stateful updates) that don't map cleanly to these primitives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federated Averaging (local SGD) as a communication-efficient baseline
rubrics_metrics.description: Federated Averaging: clients perform K local SGD steps and the server averages updated local models to form the global model; reduces communication frequency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While Federated Averaging addresses data locality and communication constraints, it introduces algorithmic challenges for convergence analysis (especially with non-IID data) and for choosing hyperparameters like K and client-sampling M.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of IID assumptions for theoretical baseline analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: IID data across clients simplifies theoretical convergence analysis and provides a baseline for understanding the impact of non-IID data, even though IID rarely holds in practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyses often assume IID to derive rates; designers must be cautious translating IID results to realistic, heterogeneous settings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of wall-clock runtime and topology-dependent communication delays
rubrics_metrics.description: Optimization and topology design should factor in actual wall-clock runtime per SGD iteration, since topology (node degree) affects per-iteration communication delay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many theoretical works ignore runtime implications; methods like MATCHA target reducing per-iteration delay by decomposing graphs into parallel matchings and selecting subgraphs smartly.
